title: Corporate Exit: The Anatomy of Separation
body:
Leaving a major corporation in Meridian 88 is a process that has more in common with exiting a sovereign state than with resigning from a conventional employer. The legal complexity of corporate separation stems from the accumulation of instruments signed during induction and throughout employment: non-compete clauses that typically prohibit employment in overlapping functional roles within competitor organizations for periods of two to five years, non-solicitation agreements covering both clients and colleagues, intellectual property assignment clauses that survive termination indefinitely, neural data retention agreements that allow the corporation to retain copies of work-related interface logs permanently, and in many cases, residency transition requirements that give the employee thirty to ninety days to vacate corporate housing and disenroll dependents from corporate schools.

The mechanics of the separation process itself are managed through a structured protocol called 'offboarding' in most corporate HR frameworks. This process begins the moment a separation decision is made — whether voluntary resignation or employer-initiated termination — and involves a sequence of steps designed to minimize information leakage and transition the employee out of the corporate ecosystem with minimal disruption to operational continuity. Interface access is typically revoked within hours of the separation decision, before the employee has had an opportunity to copy personal data from corporate systems. This includes, in most cases, contacts, personal communications sent through internal platforms, and any personal files stored on corporate servers. Employees who have spent years using corporate infrastructure as their primary digital environment often find themselves effectively digitally dispossessed at the moment of exit.

The indenture settlement component of separation is frequently the most practically significant. Because most corporate employees carry indenture balances from augmentation upgrades, housing advances, and training costs, separation typically triggers an immediate settlement calculation. Voluntary resignation in most contracts accelerates the full remaining indenture balance to immediate due status, creating an exit cost that can range from a few months' salary for junior employees to several years' equivalent for senior technical staff who have received significant augmentation investment. Corporations offer structured settlement plans, but these plans typically require the departing employee to continue making payments that tie their financial life to the former employer for years after exit. Employees who cannot afford immediate settlement and who decline the structured payment plan face referral to the Meridian Commercial Debt Enforcement system, which operates under zone sovereignty frameworks that give corporations significant enforcement tools.

For employees who exit and seek employment in Meridian 88's unaffiliated zones or with smaller corporate entities, the transition involves a fundamental recalibration of daily life. Leaving a corporate residential zone means finding housing in a market that is both more expensive and less reliably maintained. Losing access to corporate healthcare means transitioning to the municipal system at whatever citizenship tier the employee holds — and it is worth noting that extended corporate employment can in some cases actually erode a citizen's engagement with the municipal tier system, leaving them with lapsed documentation or outdated tier classifications that require time and money to restore. The cumulative effect of corporate dependency is most visible at the moment of its removal: employees who have lived inside the corporate ecosystem for five years or more often describe the exit experience as disorienting in ways that go far beyond the practical difficulties of the transition.
